Let $m,n$ be nonnegative integers, $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $b\in\mathbb R^m$, and $c\in\mathbb R^n$. The standard-form minimization linear program with data $(A,b,c)$ is
$$\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}.$$
Its feasible set is $P(A,b)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x_j\ge0\text{ for every }j\}$, and a feasible $x$ is optimal if $c^{\mathsf T}x\le c^{\mathsf T}z$ for every $z\in P(A,b)$. The notation $x\ge0$ is componentwise. The revised-simplex basis algorithms on this page require a full-row-rank matrix, meaning $\operatorname{rank}(A)=m$; a rank-deficient raw system must first be reduced by exact row operations, with inconsistent rows reported as infeasible. For $m=0$, the empty system has its usual zero-dimensional interpretation.

A vector $q\in\mathbb R^m$ satisfying $A^{\mathsf T}q\ge0$ and $b^{\mathsf T}q<0$ is called a **Farkas infeasibility certificate** for this sign convention. Indeed, any feasible $x\ge0$ would give $b^{\mathsf T}q=x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}q\ge0$.

Use the standard-form problem of [[def-revised-simplex-standard-form-linear-program]]. Assume $A$ has full row rank $m$. An ordered basis is a list $B=(B_1,\ldots,B_m)$ of distinct column indices for which the square matrix $A_B=[a_{B_1}\ \cdots\ a_{B_m}]$ is invertible. Write $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\{B_1,\ldots,B_m\}$ and $c_B=(c_{B_1},\ldots,c_{B_m})^{\mathsf T}$. The basic vector $x(B)$ is defined by $x_B(B)=A_B^{-1}b$ and $x_j(B)=0$ for $j\in N$; the basis is primal feasible, and $x(B)$ is a basic feasible solution, exactly when $A_B^{-1}b\ge0$.

The basis multiplier is $y(B)=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B$. For every column $j$, its reduced cost is $\bar c_j=c_j-a_j^{\mathsf T}y(B)$. In particular, $\bar c_{B_i}=0$ for each basic index. The basis is dual feasible when $\bar c_j\ge0$ for every $j\in N$. When $m=0$, take the empty basis and the empty multiplier; these formulas remain meaningful.

A primal-feasible basis is **degenerate** if some basic coordinate is zero. A simplex pivot is **degenerate** if its ratio-test step length is zero.

derivations.claim: If the support columns indexed by $S(x)$ are dependent, choose a nonzero vector $d$ supported on $S(x)$ with $Ad=0$. Since each $x_j>0$ on this finite support, choose $\varepsilon>0$ smaller than $x_j/|d_j|$ for every nonzero $d_j$. Then $x+\varepsilon d$ and $x-\varepsilon d$ are distinct nonnegative solutions of $Az=b$, and their midpoint is $x$; hence $x$ is not extreme.

Suppose the support columns are independent and $x=tu+(1-t)v$ for feasible $u,v$ and $0<t<1$. For $j\notin S(x)$, nonnegativity and $x_j=0$ force $u_j=v_j=0$. Thus $u-v$ is supported on $S(x)$ and $A(u-v)=0$; independence forces $u=v$, and the convex-combination identity then gives $u=v=x$. This proves extremality under its stated definition.

If the support columns of a feasible point are dependent, take $d$ as in step 1.1 and choose its sign so some $d_j<0$. With $t=\min_{d_j<0}x_j/(-d_j)>0$, the point $x+td$ remains feasible, remains nonnegative, and has strictly fewer positive coordinates. Repeating this support reduction at most $n$ times gives a feasible point whose support columns are independent.

Because $A$ has rank $m$, its columns span $\mathbb R^m$. Extend the independent support columns from step 2.1 to $m$ independent columns of $A$ by repeatedly taking the least-index column outside their current span; assigning zero to each added coordinate makes the reduced point the basic vector of that basis. It is therefore a basic feasible solution. When $m=0$, support reduction gives the zero vector and the empty list is the required basis.

A basic feasible solution has support contained in an independent basis, so its support columns are independent and step 1.2 makes it extreme. Conversely, an extreme feasible point has independent support by step 1.1 and extends to a basis by step 3.1. Thus the three stated conditions are equivalent, and step 3.1 proves existence whenever $P(A,b)$ is nonempty.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be $C^2$. Let $p,m\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed; when the target
dimension is positive, let $h:U\to\mathbb R^p$ and
$g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):U\to\mathbb R^m$ be componentwise $C^2$, and when it
is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The $C^2$ inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},
$$
and
$$
\mathcal L_C(x)=\{d:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\}.
$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with
$Dg_i(x)w<0$ for every active $i$; the latter condition is vacuous if
$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition
just stated. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is the stationarity,
feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity system below.

For $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, the Lagrangian and KKT
system are
$$
L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x),
$$
$$
h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\le0,\quad \lambda\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \nabla_xL(x,\nu,\lambda)=0.
$$
The critical cone for a KKT tuple is
$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap
\{d:\nabla f(x)^Td=0\}$. These definitions use the differentiability and
gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

[[def-kkt-residual-and-normal-cone]].

If some $d_i>0$, set $\theta=\min_{d_i>0}x_{B_i}/d_i$. Each ratio is nonnegative, the finite nonempty index set has a minimum, and $x_B-\theta d\ge0$: rows with $d_i>0$ satisfy the ratio bound, while rows with $d_i\le0$ do not decrease. The entering component is $\theta\ge0$, so $x+\theta r$ is feasible.

For any minimizing row $i$, replacing column $B_i$ by $a_j$ gives a basis: in coordinates of $A_B$, the replacement column is $d$, whose $i$th entry is positive, so expansion along that column gives a nonzero determinant. The unique basic vector of the new basis is $x+\theta r$, because that vector satisfies the constraints and has zero on the remaining nonbasic variables.

The objective change is $c^{\mathsf T}(x+\theta r)-c^{\mathsf T}x=\theta c^{\mathsf T}r=\theta\bar c_j$. Since $\theta\ge0$ and $\bar c_j<0$, it is nonpositive and is zero exactly when $\theta=0$, the degenerate-pivot case.

If $n=0$, the feasible set contains only the empty vector, so its feasible basic vector is optimal. Suppose $n\ge1$. Set $U=\mathbb R^n$, $f(z)=c^{\mathsf T}z$, $h(z)=Az-b$, $g_j(z)=-z_j$, $
u=-y(B)$, and $\lambda=c-A^{\mathsf T}y(B)$. The open convex domain is $U=\mathbb R^n$, and the affine functions are differentiable and convex. abla f(x)+A^{\mathsf T}

Let $F$ be a field, and let $m,n,s\in\mathbb N$, where $\mathbb N$ includes
$0$. A **compressed sparse row (CSR) record** for an $m$ by $n$ matrix over
$F$ consists of integer arrays $r=(r_0,\ldots,r_m)$ and
$c=(c_0,\ldots,c_{s-1})$, and a value array $v=(v_0,\ldots,v_{s-1})\in F^s$,
satisfying

$$r_0=0,\qquad 0=r_0\le r_1\le\cdots\le r_m=s,\qquad 0\le c_t<n\quad(0\le t<s).$$

For each row $i<m$, its **stored entries** are the indices
$t$ with $r_i\le t<r_{i+1}$. The row is empty exactly when
$r_i=r_{i+1}$. Repeated column indices within one row and stored values
$v_t=0_F$ are permitted; each such entry remains a separate stored entry.

The represented matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ is defined entrywise by

$$A_{ij}:=\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}v_t\qquad(0\le i<m,\ 0\le j<n),$$

where $\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}$ is $1_F$ when $c_t=j$ and $0_F$ otherwise, and an
empty sum is $0_F$. Repeated entries in column $j$ are therefore added. The
number $s$ is the **stored-entry count**; it is not in general the number of
nonzero entries of $A$.

A CSR record is **canonical** when no row repeats a column and no stored value
is zero. In that case every nonzero matrix entry is stored exactly once and
$s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)$, where $\operatorname{nnz}(A)$ denotes the number of
nonzero entries of $A$. If $m=0$, the endpoint conditions force $s=0$ and the
row-pointer array has its single entry $r_0=0$. If $n=0$, the column-index
condition forces $s=0$ as well.

derivations.claim: The intervals $[r_i,r_{i+1})$ are disjoint and, because $r_0=0$ and $r_m=s$, their union is $[0,s)$. After processing the first $k$ stored indices, the accumulator satisfies $w_j=\sum_{0\le t<k,\ c_t=j}v_ty_{i(t)}$: this holds at $k=0$, and the next update adds exactly its one summand to component $c_k$.

At $k=s$, for each column $j$ the CSR reconstruction in [F2] gives $(A^{\mathsf T}y)_j=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}A_{ij}y_i=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}\mathbf1_{c_t=j}v_ty_i=\sum_{0\le t<s,\ c_t=j}v_ty_{i(t)}=w_j$. The finite row intervals partition the stored indices, so the reindexing counts every stored term once; real multiplication distributes over finite sums. By [F1], $c-w$ is the reduced-cost vector when $y=y(B)$.

Each of the $s$ updates performs one multiplication and one addition, and initialization and final subtraction each touch exactly $n$ coordinates. Return these exact values and $|g|$ as the exact primal-dual objective difference for the stored data. Return `verified-optimal-for-stored-data` exactly when $\hat x\ge0$, $r_p=0$, $r_d\ge0$, and $g=0$. The exact arithmetic is a verification procedure for a candidate produced by a floating-point solver; it does not define a basis factorization or bound uncertainty in data before they were stored. If a statement about pre-rounded data is required, separate certified input intervals must be supplied and propagated. The procedure makes no operation-count or runtime claim.

$$g=x^{\mathsf T}r_d+y^{\mathsf T}r_p,$$
and consequently
$$|g|\le \|x\|_1\|r_d\|_\infty+\|y\|_1\|r_p\|_\infty.$$
Here $\|z\|_1=\sum_i|z_i|$ and $\|z\|_\infty=\max_i|z_i|$, with both norms equal to zero on the empty vector. Input finite stored binary data for the standard-form LP of [[def-revised-simplex-basis-dictionary]], with full-row-rank $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, a candidate ordered basis $B$ of $m$ distinct in-range indices, and a nonnegative integer budget $K$ of basis evaluations. Stored values represent their exact dyadic rationals. Invalid dimensions, nonfinite inputs or repeated/out-of-range basis indices return `invalid-input`. Nonsingularity of $C=A_B$ must be established as part of an admitted basis input; a numerical rank threshold is not such an establishment. A basis whose validity is unavailable returns `basis-validity-inconclusive`.

A caller may request a primal or dual simplex transition after an audit, or only an audit. It may supply a finite sequence of transition records, one for each requested basis replacement, from [[alg-revised-primal-simplex-bland-rule]] or [[alg-revised-dual-simplex-with-finite-budget]]. A transition record has fields `mode` (primal or dual), `basis_before` (the ordered current basis, with its validity witness), `leaving_position` $i$, and `entering_index` $j$; it is checked rather than trusted as already verified. The initial basis and each record's `basis_before` must carry the validity witness described here. After a replacement, its checked nonzero pivot coefficient establishes the new basis; any next transition record must carry its own checked validity witness.

An admitted basis input includes either an exact rational inverse witness $G$ with $CG=GC=I_m$, checked exactly, or a rational matrix $H$ and rational $q$ with $0\le q<1$ and $\|I_m-HC\|_\infty\le q$, also checked exactly. For matrices with at least one row, $\|M\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_j|M_{ij}|$; the empty matrix has norm $0$. For vectors it is the maximum absolute coordinate, with empty value $0$. For $m=0$, the empty inverse witness satisfies the identities. If neither validity certificate is verified, return `basis-validity-inconclusive` before factorization. A numerical rank threshold is never a validity certificate.

With an exact inverse witness, first compare `basis_before` with the current ordered basis exactly. Then check a transition by exact rational arithmetic: compute $x_B=Gb$, $y=G^{\mathsf T}c_B$, $d_k=Ga_k$ for every nonbasic $k$, and $\bar c_k=c_k-a_k^{\mathsf T}y$. A primal record is admissible exactly when $x_B\ge0$, $j$ is the least-index nonbasic column with $\bar c_j<0$, some $d_{rj}>0$, and $i$ minimizes $x_{B_r}/d_{rj}$ over rows with $d_{rj}>0$, with ties resolved by least basic-variable index. A dual record is admissible exactly when every nonbasic $\bar c_k\ge0$, $B_i$ is the least-index basic variable with $x_{B_i}<0$, $d_{ij}<0$, and $j$ minimizes $\bar c_k/(-d_{ik})$ over nonbasic $k$ with $d_{ik}<0$, with ties resolved by least variable index. In either case, the checked nonzero pivot coefficient proves the replacement basis nonsingular.

Certified rational enclosures may instead establish a transition. For each current $D=C$ and $D=C^{\mathsf T}$, provide rational $H_D,q_D,M_D$ with $0\le q_D<1$, $\|I_m-H_DD\|_\infty\le q_D$, and $M_D\ge\|H_D\|_\infty/(1-q_D)$; verify these inequalities exactly. For each solve $Dz=r$, combine its returned candidate $\widehat z$ and a rational upper bound $\eta$ for its Step 3 residual bound to form the coordinate intervals $[\widehat z_\ell-M_D\eta,\widehat z_\ell+M_D\eta]$. For closed rational intervals $I=[a,b]$ and $J=[c,d]$, use $I+J=[a+c,b+d]$, $I-J=[a-d,b-c]$, $IJ=[\min\{ac,ad,bc,bd\},\max\{ac,ad,bc,bd\}]$, and $I/J=I\cdot[\min\{1/c,1/d\},\max\{1/c,1/d\}]$ when $0\notin J$; division is undefined otherwise. Evaluate dot products, reduced costs, and ratio expressions with these exact rational endpoint operations. First compare `basis_before` with the current ordered basis exactly. An interval proves a sign or order only when its endpoints imply that relation. If a ratio comparison is not decided by interval endpoints, return `pivot-inconclusive` unless an exact inverse witness $G$ is supplied for the current basis; with $G$, compute the exact rational ratios and compare them exactly, resolving equality by the least-index rule. Admit the record only when the required signs and comparisons, including all least-index rules, are proved. If a needed sign, ratio comparison, or basis match is not established, return `pivot-inconclusive` with the current basis and its last completed audit, without changing the basis.

For $m\ge1$, use the operationwise arithmetic of [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]], with $0<u<1$, $mu<1$, $(m+3)u<1$, and $\gamma_{m+3}<1/8$. All nonzero exact intermediates must be normal. Norms and certificate expressions below are evaluated exactly or by certified upward bounds; failure to obtain a finite valid bound is a numerical failure. Process the following loop:

1. Maintain an attempt counter $t$, initially $0$. If $t=K$, return `budget-exhausted` with the current basis, the last completed audit if any, and the basis to which that audit belongs. Otherwise set $t\leftarrow t+1$ before starting this basis evaluation. Every budget, numerical-failure, basis-validity-inconclusive, or pivot-inconclusive return includes the current basis and identifies the basis associated with any retained audit; state explicitly when no audit exists.
2. Separately for $D=C=A_B$ and $D=C^{\mathsf T}$, copy the current stored entries into a working matrix $W$. For $k=1,\ldots,m$, set $r=m-k+1$, take the active column $x=W_{k:m,k}$ and trailing block $T=W_{k:m,k+1:m}$, and call [[alg-scaled-householder-reflector-formation-and-application]] once on $(x,T)$. On success, save its reflector data and replace the active block $W_{k:m,k:m}$ by its returned output, which writes the new diagonal entry and exact zeros below it; leave earlier rows and columns unchanged. If $x=0$, save an identity marker and leave the trailing block unchanged. Stop with `numerical-failure` at the first failed call, recording the factorization, column $k$, and failure stage. The final $W$ is the computed upper-triangular factor $\widehat R_D$.

   To apply these stored reflectors to any right-hand side $s$, start with $z=s$ and visit $k=1,\ldots,m$ in that same order. Skip an identity marker. Otherwise, on the active suffix $z_{k:m}$ compute the sequential rounded dot $d=\operatorname{fl}(v_k^{\mathsf T}z_{k:m})$, then $p=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau_k v_k)$, $u=\operatorname{fl}(p\,d)$ componentwise, and $z_{k:m}=\operatorname{fl}(z_{k:m}-u)$ componentwise, using the operation order of [[alg-scaled-householder-reflector-formation-and-application]] without a column overwrite. Stop at the first failure and record the right-hand side, reflector index, and failure stage. For $Dz=s$, apply this replay to obtain the transformed right-hand side and solve $\widehat R_D\widehat z=z$ by descending substitution: for $i=m,\ldots,1$, sequentially compute $t_i=\operatorname{fl}(\sum_{j=i+1}^m(\widehat R_D)_{ij}\widehat z_j)$, $h_i=\operatorname{fl}(z_i-t_i)$, and $\widehat z_i=\operatorname{fl}(h_i/(\widehat R_D)_{ii})$. A zero diagonal or any failed operation returns `numerical-failure` with the solve and row index. Reuse the $C$ factorization for $\widehat x_B$ and every nonbasic direction $\widehat d_j$; reuse the $C^{\mathsf T}$ factorization for $\widehat y$. Never substitute a rounded dense orthogonal product for the exact orthogonal representative in the proof. After every admitted basis replacement discard both factorizations and recompute; no rank-one factorization-update implementation is claimed.
3. Independently certify each returned solve for its actual current matrix $D=C$ or $C^{\mathsf T}$ and right-hand side $r$. Compute $\widehat v=\operatorname{fl}(D\widehat z)$ and $\widehat w=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-r)$ by the sequential products/subtraction of [[lem-rounded-linear-and-normal-residual-certificates]]. Put
$$g_m=\frac{1+6u}{1-(m-1)u}-1,\qquad W=g_m\|D\|_F\|\widehat z\|_2+u(\|\widehat v\|_2+\|r\|_2).$$
With the local coefficient $\kappa_m$ of [[lem-scaled-householder-step-meets-local-backward-error-premise]], put
$$\beta=(1+\kappa_m)^m-1,\qquad \beta_D=\beta+\gamma_{m+3}(1+\beta),$$
and report the valid upper bound
$$\eta(D,r,\widehat z)=\min\{\|\widehat w\|_2+W,\ \beta_D\|D\|_F\|\widehat z\|_2+\beta\|r\|_2\}.$$
A finite concrete certificate option uses exact rational arithmetic on the stored dyadic entries and a rational upper bound for $u$ satisfying all displayed admissibility inequalities. Use $\|v\|_2\le\sum_i|v_i|$ and $\|D\|_F\le\sum_{i,j}|D_{ij}|$ as rational upper bounds for every norm in the two nonnegative expressions. For the local coefficient, substitute $\bar e_m=(1+u)^{m+3}-1$ for $e_m=(1+u)^{m/2+3}-1$ in the source formula: put $\bar d_m=\bar e_m+u(2+\bar e_m)$, $a_m=(1+u)/(1-u)^m-1$, $g_m^{\rm QR}=mu/(1-mu)$, $c_m=2((1+a_m)(1+u)^2(1+g_m^{\rm QR})-1)$, and $\bar\kappa_m=\max\{\bar e_m+8\bar d_m,(1+u)c_m+3u\}$. These are rational upper bounds because $m+3\ge m/2+3$ and all constituent nonnegative formulas increase in their arguments. Then $\bar\beta=(1+\bar\kappa_m)^m-1$ and $\bar\beta_D=\bar\beta+\gamma_{m+3}(1+\bar\beta)$ are rational upper bounds for the QR coefficients. Compute both candidate bounds by finite exact rational sums/products/powers and take their minimum as the returned $\eta$. This implements the certificate without a norm oracle; other finite certified upper-bound procedures are allowed. Any factorization, substitution, dot, subtraction, range or certificate failure returns `numerical-failure`, with its stage and the last completed audit; it returns no certificate for the failed solve.
4. Embed $\widehat x_B$ in $\widehat x\in\mathbb R^n$ with zero nonbasic entries, and call [[alg-revised-simplex-residual-audit]] on these actual stored $\widehat x,\widehat y$. Retain its exact $r_p=A\widehat x-b$, $r_d=c-A^{\mathsf T}\widehat y$, objective difference $g$, and audit status together with all solve residual bounds. `basis-solves-residual-certified` means only that the returned bounds certify those linear equations; any requested thresholds must also be checked before declaring them met. `verified-optimal-for-stored-data` is issued only by the exact audit's primal/sign/zero-gap checks. Other completed candidates remain `candidate-only`; small residuals or a failed/ambiguous pivot never certify infeasibility.
5. Return if audit-only mode or the caller has no further transition. Otherwise compare the next record with the current basis and apply the exact or enclosure admission predicate above. A failed or unresolved predicate returns `pivot-inconclusive` or `basis-validity-inconclusive`, retaining the current basis and last completed audit. On admission, replace position $i$ by $j$, discard both factorizations, and continue at Step 1. Exact driver invariants remain those of the existing driver, not consequences of successful floating solves.

For $m=0$, skip QR and substitution: the basis and multiplier are empty, every direction is the empty vector, and their basis-equation residuals and solve bounds $\eta$ are zero. Evaluate the existing exact audit with $\widehat x=0$; no basis replacement is possible. The budget and invalid-input branches remain in force.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $m\ge n\ge1$, have full column rank. Successful scaled Householder QR gives the exactly orthonormal reduced representative $\widehat Q$ and computed triangular $\widehat R$ with
$$A+\Delta_Q=\widehat Q\widehat R,\qquad \|\Delta_Q\|_F\le\beta_Q\|A\|_F,\qquad \beta_Q=(1+\kappa_m)^n-1,$$
where $\kappa_m$ is the proved local-step coefficient. Apply the stored reflectors to $b$ by rounded rank-one updates and let $\widehat y$ be the first $n$ coordinates. Set $\beta_b=\beta_Q$. Alternatively, if an explicitly supplied exactly orthonormal $\widehat Q$ has entries admissible as arithmetic inputs and $\widehat y=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat Q^Tb)$ uses sequential rounded dots, set $\beta_b=\sqrt n\,\gamma_m$. Solve $\widehat R\widehat x=\widehat y$ by successful rounded back substitution. Suppose $mu<1$ and $\gamma_{n+3}<1/8$. There exist $\delta b$ and upper triangular $\Delta R$ with
$$(\widehat R+\Delta R)\widehat x=\widehat Q^T(b+\delta b),\qquad \|\delta b\|_2\le\beta_b\|b\|_2,\qquad \|\Delta R\|_F\le\gamma_{n+3}\|\widehat R\|_F.$$
If $\widehat R+\Delta R$ is nonsingular, $\widehat x$ is the unique least-squares solution for $\widetilde A=\widehat Q(\widehat R+\Delta R)$ and $\widetilde b=b+\delta b$. The relative matrix perturbation is at most $\beta_Q+\gamma_{n+3}(1+\beta_Q)$; the right-hand perturbation is at most $\beta_b$. For fixed $m,n$, both perturbation coefficients are $O(u)$. If additionally $\beta_Q\le19\gamma_{n+3}/(1+\gamma_{n+3})$ and $\beta_b\le20\gamma_{n+3}$, both relative data perturbation bounds are at most $20\gamma_{n+3}$. These two coefficient comparisons are additional checks; they do not follow from $mu<1$ and $\gamma_{n+3}<1/8$ alone. Success and nonsingularity are explicit hypotheses.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $x\in\mathbb F^n$, $y\in\mathbb F^m$ have stored real or complex entries, with $m,n\ge1$. Use the operationwise arithmetic model, successful sequential dot products, and $0<u<1$ with $(\max(m,n)-1)u<1$. Define
$$g_k=\frac{1+6u}{1-(k-1)u}-1,\qquad F=\|A\|_F,\quad X=\|x\|_2,\quad Y=\|y\|_2.$$
For $\widehat v=\operatorname{fl}(Ax)$ and $\widehat w=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-y)$, put $V=g_nFX$ and $W=V+u(\|\widehat v\|_2+Y)$. Then
$$\|\widehat w-(Ax-y)\|_2\le W.$$
For a stored real $\lambda>0$, also compute $\widehat z=\operatorname{fl}(A^*\widehat w)$, $\widehat l=\operatorname{fl}(\lambda x)$ and $\widehat r=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat z+\widehat l)$, rounding scalar multiplication componentwise. The exact intended normal residual $r=A^*(Ax-y)+\lambda x$ satisfies
$$\|\widehat r-r\|_2\le\rho:=FW+g_mF\|\widehat w\|_2+u\lambda X+u(\|\widehat z\|_2+\|\widehat l\|_2).$$
Norms in these certificates mean exact norms or certified upper bounds. Uncontrolled rounding of the certificate itself is not authorized. The linear bound applies columnwise to certify $\|I-AB\|_2\le\|I-AB\|_F$ from stored basis-solve columns $B$.

For a real standard-form problem with $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ and candidate vectors $x\in\mathbb R^n$, $y\in\mathbb R^m$, define $r_p=Ax-b$, $r_d=c-A^{\mathsf T}y$, and $g=c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y$. When the data and candidates are finite stored binary floating-point values, [[alg-revised-simplex-residual-audit]] computes precisely these quantities, interpreting the stored values as exact dyadic rationals. For all the stated real data,
$$g=x^{\mathsf T}r_d+y^{\mathsf T}r_p,$$
and consequently
$$|g|\le \|x\|_1\|r_d\|_\infty+\|y\|_1\|r_p\|_\infty.$$
Here $\|z\|_1=\sum_i|z_i|$ and $\|z\|_\infty=\max_i|z_i|$, with both norms equal to zero on the empty vector. This bounds the primal-dual objective difference; when either vector is infeasible it does not bound distance to an optimal value. If $Ax=b$, $x\ge0$, $c-A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0$, and $g=0$, then $x$ is optimal.
